claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The sapA gene has 9-fold higher ribosome occupancy with S-ribosomes than with C-ribosomes.
claims.source: The same phenomenon was observed on rbsK (7-fold higher RO) and mreB (10-fold higher RO) with the O-ribosome and on sapA (9-fold higher RO) and rsmH (4-fold higher RO) with the S-ribosome (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The rsmH gene has 4-fold higher ribosome occupancy with S-ribosomes than with C-ribosomes.
claims.source: The same phenomenon was observed on rbsK (7-fold higher RO) and mreB (10-fold higher RO) with the O-ribosome and on sapA (9-fold higher RO) and rsmH (4-fold higher RO) with the S-ribosome (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: All three ASD mutants essentially act as general loss of function mutants.
claims.source: These examples are quite rare, however, because endogenous genes have evolved to interact with the canonical ASD and so the probability of finding a sequence with strong complementarity to the mutant ASD at just the right position is relatively low. Indeed, our data are most consistent with the conclusion that all three ASD mutants essentially act as general loss of function mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that few genes show increased translation with mutant ribosomes.

claims.claim: Data from canonical (C) ribosomes showed only a very weak correlation between ribosome occupancy and SD strength.
claims.source: However, our analysis of data from canonical (C) ribosomes showed only a very weak correlation (Figure 2A), consistent with previous reports from ribosome profiling studies (Li et al., 2014) showing that SD strength has little power to predict ribosome occupancy in E. coli.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: RO values from the three ASD mutants (S, O, and A) showed a robust negative correlation with SD affinity for the wild-type ASD sequence.
claims.source: Strikingly, the RO values from the three ASD mutants (S, O, and A) showed a robust negative correlation with SD affinity for the wild-type ASD sequence (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: ASD mutant ribosomes translate genes with weak SD motifs better than genes with strong SD motifs.
claims.source: In other words, ASD mutant ribosomes translate genes with weak SD motifs better than genes with strong SD motifs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the negative correlation between RO and SD strength for mutant ribosomes.

claims.claim: ∆logRO values plotted as a function of SD-ASD affinity show a strong linear correlation with SD-ASD affinity for each of the mutants.
claims.source: When ∆logRO values are plotted as a function of SD-ASD affinity (-∆G) using the wild-type ASD sequence, we observe a strong linear correlation with SD-ASD affinity for each of the mutants (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Genes with strong SD motifs are translated better by ribosomes with the canonical ASD than by ASD-mutant ribosomes.
claims.source: As expected, genes with strong SD motifs are translated better by ribosomes with the canonical ASD than by ASD-mutant ribosomes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ∆logRO analysis showing positive correlation with SD strength.

claims.claim: Genes with the highest ∆logRO have the strongest SD affinity in the −15 to −6 region.
claims.source: The fact that we observe this correlation validates our calculations of SD strength; analysis of the distance of SD motifs from the start codon confirms that genes with the highest ∆logRO have the strongest SD affinity in the −15 to −6 region as shown in previous studies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Retapamulin traps newly-initiated ribosomes in bacteria.
claims.source: Two antibiotics were recently shown to similarly specifically trap initiation complexes in bacteria: Onc112 and retapamulin (Meydan et al., 2019; Weaver et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on retapamulin.

claims.claim: Elongating wild-type (C) ribosomes are found all across the lpp gene in untreated cells.
claims.source: For example, elongating wild-type (C) ribosomes are found all across the lpp gene in untreated cells (Figure 3A, light grey), whereas they are highly enriched at the annotated start codon in retapamulin-treated cells (dark grey).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Wild-type ribosomes are highly enriched at the annotated start codon of lpp in retapamulin-treated cells.
claims.source: For example, elongating wild-type (C) ribosomes are found all across the lpp gene in untreated cells (Figure 3A, light grey), whereas they are highly enriched at the annotated start codon in retapamulin-treated cells (dark grey).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Ribosome footprints are not seen at three internal AUG codons in the lpp gene.
claims.source: As expected, ribosome footprints are not seen at three internal AUG codons, since these do not function as initiation sites.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: A-ribosomes find the correct start site in the lpp gene in retapamulin-treated cells, ignoring three other AUG codons.
claims.source: Strikingly, in retapamulin-treated cells, the A-ribosomes also find the correct start site, ignoring the three other AUG codons (Figure 3A, dark green).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Both C- and A-ribosomes are enriched at the annotated start codon of gmk in retapamulin-treated cells but not at several internal AUG codons.
claims.source: In another example, the gmk gene, both C- and A-ribosomes are enriched at the annotated start codon in retapamulin-treated cells but not at several internal AUG codons (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Both WT and mutant ribosomes select the correct, annotated start site while ignoring other AUG codons.
claims.source: In both examples, both WT and mutant ribosomes select the correct, annotated start site while ignoring other AUG codons.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Both C- and A-ribosomes show strong initiation peaks at annotated AUGs genome-wide.
claims.source: Strikingly, both the C- and A-ribosomes show strong initiation peaks at annotated AUGs (Figure 3C), whereas these peaks are absent in both samples at non-annotated AUGs (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the average ribosome footprint data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Initiation peaks are absent at non-annotated AUGs for both C- and A-ribosomes.
claims.source: Strikingly, both the C- and A-ribosomes show strong initiation peaks at annotated AUGs (Figure 3C), whereas these peaks are absent in both samples at non-annotated AUGs (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the average ribosome footprint data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Ribosomes correctly select annotated start sites genome-wide in the absence of the SD-ASD interaction.
claims.source: These results provide initial evidence that ribosomes correctly select annotated start sites genome-wide in the absence of the SD-ASD interaction.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mutant ribosomes initiate at annotated sites.

claims.claim: A, O, and S ribosomes show robust enrichment at annotated start sites with no predicted affinity for any of the three ASD mutants.
claims.source: In the subset of genes with no predicted affinity for any of the three ASD mutants (ΔG > −1), we still see robust enrichment of A, O, and S ribosomes at the annotated start sites (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the average ribosome footprint data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: All three ASD variants initiate at annotated start sites, arguing against serendipitous base-pairing between the mRNA and the mutant ASD sequences.
claims.source: Since all three ASD variants initiate at annotated start sites, these data argue against the possibility that serendipitous base-pairing between the mRNA and the mutant ASD sequences explains this enrichment.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that all three different mutants initiate at the same sites.

claims.claim: Robust start peaks are observed for each ASD variant ribosome at annotated start sites with strong calculated affinity to the wild-type ASD.
claims.source: We also analyzed a set of annotated start sites with strong calculated affinity to the wild-type ASD. These sites are expected to be dependent on the SD-ASD interaction. Yet we again observed robust start peaks for each ASD variant ribosome, indicating that SD-ASD pairing is dispensable for initiation even in genes with strong SD motifs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the average ribosome footprint data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: SD-ASD pairing is dispensable for initiation even in genes with strong SD motifs.
claims.source: We also analyzed a set of annotated start sites with strong calculated affinity to the wild-type ASD. These sites are expected to be dependent on the SD-ASD interaction. Yet we again observed robust start peaks for each ASD variant ribosome, indicating that SD-ASD pairing is dispensable for initiation even in genes with strong SD motifs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mutant ribosomes initiate at sites with strong wild-type SD motifs.

claims.claim: In genes with predicted high affinity to the ASD of the O-ribosome, there was strong enrichment of A- and S-ribosomes at start codons.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that in a set of sites with predicted high affinity to the ASD of the O-ribosome, there was strong enrichment of A- and S-ribosomes at start codons, despite the differences in the ASD sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the average ribosome footprint data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: In genes with predicted high affinity to the ASD of the S-ribosome, there was strong enrichment of O- and A-ribosomes at start codons.
claims.source: Likewise, in a set of genes with predicted high affinity to the ASD of the S-ribosome, there was strong enrichment of O- and A-ribosomes at start codons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the average ribosome footprint data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Annotated initiation sites are hard-wired for initiation independent of their potential for base pairing between the mRNA and rRNA.
claims.source: Taken together, these analyses show that annotated initiation sites are hard-wired for initiation independent of their potential for base pairing between the mRNA and rRNA.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that all mutant ribosomes initiate at annotated sites regardless of predicted base-pairing potential.

claims.claim: The log2IS values from the C- and A-ribosomes have a similar distribution with medians close to 0 for non-annotated AUGs.
claims.source: The first and most general finding is that the log2IS values from the C- and A-ribosomes have a similar distribution with medians close to 0 (Figure 4B), indicating that footprints from the A-ribosomes are not enriched at non-annotated AUG codons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the initiation score distribution shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Footprints from the A-ribosomes are not enriched at non-annotated AUG codons.
claims.source: The first and most general finding is that the log2IS values from the C- and A-ribosomes have a similar distribution with medians close to 0 (Figure 4B), indicating that footprints from the A-ribosomes are not enriched at non-annotated AUG codons.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar IS distributions for C- and A-ribosomes at non-annotated AUGs.

claims.claim: Non-annotated AUG codons with high IS values for C-ribosomes also show high IS values for A-ribosomes.
claims.source: Surprisingly, this same subset of AUG codons also shows high IS values for A-ribosomes (Figure 4C), arguing that SD-ASD pairing is not the feature that explains why initiation takes place at these specific AUG triplets and not at others.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the initiation score comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: SD-ASD pairing is not the feature that explains why initiation takes place at specific non-annotated AUG triplets.
claims.source: Surprisingly, this same subset of AUG codons also shows high IS values for A-ribosomes (Figure 4C), arguing that SD-ASD pairing is not the feature that explains why initiation takes place at these specific AUG triplets and not at others.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that A-ribosomes initiate at the same non-annotated sites as C-ribosomes.

claims.claim: For non-annotated AUGs with high affinity to the ASD of the S-ribosome, the distribution of IS values for S-ribosomes closely resembled the other three ribosomes.
claims.source: For sites with high affinity to the ASD of the S-ribosome, for example, the distribution of IS values for S-ribosomes closely resembled the other three ribosomes (Figure 4E), with median values near zero.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the initiation score distribution shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The presence of a complementary Shine-Dalgarno-like sequence near an AUG codon is not sufficient to recruit S-ribosomes and generate a robust start codon peak.
claims.source: These data show that the presence of a complementary Shine-Dalgarno-like sequence near an AUG codon is not sufficient to recruit S-ribosomes and generate a robust start codon peak.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that most AUGs with high affinity to S-ribosomes do not show high IS values.

claims.claim: Non-annotated AUGs with high affinity to S-ribosomes where initiation occurs with S-ribosomes also show robust start peaks with other ribosomes with different ASD sequences.
claims.source: We selected the subset of AUGs with high affinity to S-ribosomes where initiation occurs with S-ribosomes (log2IS >1.5, dark red in Figure 4E). As expected, these high-IS sites show strong start peaks with S-ribosomes; however, the other ribosomes with different ASD sequences show robust start peaks as well (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the average ribosome footprint data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Low-IS sites that are not translated by S-ribosomes are also not translated by the other ribosomes.
claims.source: Similarly, low-IS sites that are not translated by S-ribosomes (light red in Figure 4E) are also not translated by the other ribosomes (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the average ribosome footprint data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: SD-ASD pairing does not contribute to initiation at non-annotated AUGs with high affinity to the S-ribosomes.
claims.source: The observation that SD-ASD pairing does not contribute to initiation at these sites with high affinity to the S-ribosomes also holds true for non-annotated AUGs with high affinity to the wild-type ASD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that all ribosomes behave similarly at these sites regardless of ASD sequence.

claims.claim: AUGs that recruit ribosomes and lead to initiation are hard-wired for this purpose irrespective of the strength of the mRNA-rRNA base pairing interaction.
claims.source: Once again, these data argue that AUGs that recruit ribosomes and lead to initiation are hard-wired for this purpose irrespective of the strength of the mRNA-rRNA base pairing interaction.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that initiation at specific AUGs is independent of SD-ASD pairing strength.

claims.claim: mRNA-rRNA base pairing is neither necessary nor sufficient for translational initiation.
claims.source: Taken together, these data on initiating ribosomes show that mRNA-rRNA base pairing is neither necessary nor sufficient for translational initiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective observations that mutant ribosomes initiate correctly and that complementary sequences are not sufficient for initiation.

claims.claim: Adenosines (A) are enriched at many sites within 15 nt upstream of the start codon and 5 nt downstream at annotated start sites with low affinity to the wild-type ASD.
claims.source: To avoid interference from SD motifs, we selected only annotated start sites with low affinity to the wild-type ASD (∆G > 0) and compared them to non-annotated AUG codons, most of which do not lead to initiation. We observed enrichment of adenosines (A) at many sites within 15 nt upstream of the start codon and 5 nt downstream (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the probability logo shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Replacement of A's with U's lowered GFP expression in reporter assays for yhbY, gsk, and creA* but not yeiR*.
claims.source: We observed that replacement of the A's with U's lowered GFP expression in all cases except for yeiR* which showed the weakest GFP expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the reporter assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Changing A's to C's led to complete loss of GFP fluorescence from all four AUG contexts tested in reporter assays.
claims.source: A stronger effect was observed by changing the A's to C's, which led to complete loss of GFP fluorescence from all four AUG contexts tested.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the reporter assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: A-rich sequences upstream of start codons contribute to the identification of translational start sites.
claims.source: These results support our hypothesis that A-rich sequences upstream of start codons contribute to the identification of translational start sites.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the reporter assay results showing reduced expression when A's are mutated.

claims.claim: A-rich sequences are enriched at annotated start sites compared to non-annotated AUG codons in diverse bacteria.
claims.source: The ability of A-rich sequences to promote initiation is likely not limited to E. coli: when we compared the local context of AUG codons in annotated start sites vs. non-annotated AUG codons for a set of diverse bacteria, we again saw that A-rich sequences were enriched (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the probability logos for diverse bacteria shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: For Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Flavobacterium johnsoniae, the SD signal is not observed and the enrichment of A's is particularly striking.
claims.source: For E. coli and most other species examined, the enrichment of A's was weaker than the enrichment of G's corresponding to the SD sequence, but for Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Flavobacterium johnsoniae, the SD signal is not observed and there the enrichment of A's is particularly striking.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the probability logos shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A-rich sequences are highly conserved and may serve as an important mechanism for start site selection in species lacking SD motifs.
claims.source: A-rich sequences are highly conserved and may serve as an important mechanism for start site selection in these species, while contributing broadly to more diverse species.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of A-rich sequence enrichment across diverse bacteria, particularly in species lacking SD motifs.

claims.claim: Lack of secondary structure surrounding the initiation site has the most significant correlation with protein output in reporter gene studies.
claims.source: Studies of factors that alter the expression of simplified reporter genes (involving randomization of the 5'-UTR or coding sequences) show that lack of secondary structure surrounding the initiation site has the most significant correlation with protein output (Salis et al., 2009; Kudla et al., 2009; Goodman et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous reporter gene studies.

claims.claim: For annotated initiation sites, the level of mRNA structure is significantly lower for a region 30 nt in length on both sides of the AUG codon.
claims.source: For annotated initiation sites, the level of mRNA structure is significantly lower for a region 30 nt in length on both sides of the AUG codon (shown in red) as previously reported (Del Campo et al., 2015; Burkhardt et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the SHAPE reactivity analysis shown in Figure 5E and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: mRNA structure is consistently high across a 120 nt window for non-annotated AUGs.
claims.source: In contrast, except for a sharp dip in reactivity at the aligned AUG codon due to sequence bias, we see that mRNA structure is consistently high across this window for the set of non-annotated AUGs (shown in blue).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the SHAPE reactivity analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Initiation leads to the unfolding of RNA, which facilitates initiation by another 30S subunit.
claims.source: These differences may be due in part to the ability of ribosomes to melt RNA structure during translation; indeed, initiation leads to the unfolding of RNA, which facilitates initiation by another 30S subunit (Espah Borujeni and Salis, 2016; Andreeva et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: SHAPE and DMS reactivity of mRNAs in vivo and in vitro are strongly correlated.
claims.source: But, given that SHAPE and DMS reactivity of mRNAs in vivo and in vitro are strongly correlated (Burkhardt et al., 2017; Mustoe et al., 2018), it is also likely that mRNA structure plays a causal role in setting initiation rates.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: mRNA structure likely plays a causal role in setting initiation rates.
claims.source: But, given that SHAPE and DMS reactivity of mRNAs in vivo and in vitro are strongly correlated (Burkhardt et al., 2017; Mustoe et al., 2018), it is also likely that mRNA structure plays a causal role in setting initiation rates.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between in vivo and in vitro structure measurements.

claims.claim: MS2RP can be performed on rRNA mutants expressed from plasmids and can be easily transferred to other bacteria or to eukaryotes without altering rDNA in the genome.
claims.source: Because MS2RP can be performed on rRNA mutants expressed from plasmids, the method can be easily transferred to other bacteria or to eukaryotes without altering rDNA in the genome.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the plasmid-based expression system used in the study.

claims.claim: MS2RP could be employed to characterize the functions of rRNA domains on initiation, elongation, termination, and recycling at a genome-wide level in vivo.
claims.source: In addition to the studies of the ASD sequence in 16S rRNA reported here, MS2RP could be employed to characterize the functions of rRNA domains on initiation, elongation, termination, and recycling at a genome-wide level in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications of the method.

claims.claim: Variant rRNA alleles in bacterial genomes are expressed differentially in response to changes in the environment and are proposed to have different specificities or functions.
claims.source: Of particular interest are rRNA variants in bacterial genomes that are expressed differentially in response to changes in the environment and are proposed to have different specificities or functions (Kurylo et al., 2018; Song et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Different small subunit rRNA alleles are expressed in various developmental stages in Plasmodium.
claims.source: Variant rRNA alleles have also been reported for eukaryotic cells (Parks et al., 2018); for example, different small subunit rRNA alleles are expressed in various developmental stages in Plasmodium (Gunderson et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The functions of the highly variable rRNA expansion segments in eukaryotes are poorly understood.
claims.source: In addition, the functions of the highly variable rRNA expansion segments in eukaryotes are poorly understood (Spahn et al., 2001; Anger et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: MS2RP could be a powerful tool to elucidate the activities of various subpopulations of variant or mutated rRNAs.
claims.source: MS2RP could be a powerful tool to elucidate the activities of various subpopulations of variant or mutated rRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications of the method.

claims.claim: The binding of wild-type ribosomes to mRNAs with strong SD motifs may occlude their ribosome-binding sites, preventing mutant ribosomes from initiating.
claims.source: There are two possible explanations for this negative correlation. It may be that the binding of wild-type ribosomes to mRNAs with strong SD motifs occludes their ribosome-binding sites, preventing mutant ribosomes from initiating and efficiently translating these genes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed negative correlation.

claims.claim: mRNA structure and other features may outweigh the impact of SD motifs, masking their effects in conventional ribosome profiling studies.
claims.source: Alternatively, mRNA structure and other features may outweigh the impact of SD motifs, masking their effects, explaining why conventional ribosome profiling studies failed to observe correlations between SD strength and ribosome occupancy.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why previous studies did not observe SD correlations.

claims.claim: SD motifs are underrepresented within ORFs in order to avoid spurious initiation at internal start codons.
claims.source: Consistent with such a view, SD motifs are underrepresented within ORFs in order to avoid spurious initiation at internal start codons (Hockenberry et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Local mRNA structure and RNA folding kinetics must play a critical role in allowing ribosomes to find the start codon.
claims.source: What, then, are other mechanisms that could be used for start codon selection? Local mRNA structure and RNA folding kinetics clearly must play a critical role in allowing ribosomes to find the start codon.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SD motifs are not necessary for start site selection and from established knowledge about mRNA structure effects.

claims.claim: The prevalence of A's in A-rich sequences may alter the mRNA dynamics; A-rich sequences tend to have less secondary structure than GC-rich sequences.
claims.source: The mechanism by which A-rich sequences enhance initiation is not clear. The prevalence of A's may alter the mRNA dynamics; A-rich sequences tend to have less secondary structure than GC-rich sequences.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how A-rich sequences might function.

claims.claim: Replacing A's with U's in several reporters reduced translation levels even though U's are similarly not expected to yield strong structures.
claims.source: We note however that replacing A's with U's in several reporters reduced translation levels even though the U's are similarly not expected to yield strong structures.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the reporter assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Ribosomal components may interact specifically with A's close to the start codon that are bound inside the ribosome during initiation.
claims.source: A second possibility is that ribosomal components may interact specifically with A's close to the start codon that are bound inside the ribosome during initiation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how A-rich sequences might function.

claims.claim: Mutation of a particular A at the −3 position reduces expression in reporter assays.
claims.source: Fredrick and co-workers used reporter assays to show that mutation of a particular A at the −3 position reduces expression; this result is intriguing because the classic Kozak sequence (GCC(A/G)CCAUG) that promotes high levels of translation in eukaryotes also contains a purine at position −3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to work by Fredrick and co-workers.

claims.claim: The classic Kozak sequence (GCC(A/G)CCAUG) that promotes high levels of translation in eukaryotes contains a purine at position −3.
claims.source: Fredrick and co-workers used reporter assays to show that mutation of a particular A at the −3 position reduces expression; this result is intriguing because the classic Kozak sequence (GCC(A/G)CCAUG) that promotes high levels of translation in eukaryotes also contains a purine at position −3.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the Kozak sequence.

claims.claim: A-rich sequences have been reported to enhance translation in a variety of eukaryotic contexts including Drosophila and wheat germ and reticulocyte lysates.
claims.source: A-rich sequences have been reported to enhance translation in a variety of eukaryotic contexts includingDrosophilaand wheat germ and reticulocyte lysates (Ranjan and Hasnain, 1995; Sano et al., 2002; Suzuki et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: A-rich sequences may interact with conserved elements of the ribosome across the domains of life.
claims.source: It may be that A-rich sequences interact with conserved elements of the ribosome across the domains of life.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the mechanism of A-rich sequence function.

claims.claim: A's further from the start codon (10–20 nt upstream) may interact with bacteria-specific ribosomal protein S1.
claims.source: A's further from the start codon (10–20 nt upstream) may interact with bacteria-specific ribosomal protein S1.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the mechanism of A-rich sequence function.

claims.claim: bS1 preferably binds to A/U-rich sequence elements upstream of SD sequences.
claims.source: bS1 preferably binds to A/U-rich sequence elements upstream of SD sequences (Boni et al., 1991; Komarova et al., 2005) and is thought to unwind mRNA structure to induce initiation (Qu et al., 2012; Duval et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: bS1 is thought to unwind mRNA structure to induce initiation.
claims.source: bS1 preferably binds to A/U-rich sequence elements upstream of SD sequences (Boni et al., 1991; Komarova et al., 2005) and is thought to unwind mRNA structure to induce initiation (Qu et al., 2012; Duval et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Not all bacteria utilize SD motifs to promote translational initiation—SD motifs are notably lacking in Bacteroidetes and Cyanobacteria.
claims.source: Our findings have broad implications for the evolution of translational mechanisms in bacteria. Not all bacteria utilize SD motifs to promote translational initiation—SD motifs are notably lacking in Bacteroidetes and Cyanobacteria.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by previous studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The prevalence of SD motifs is a feature of the genome in general and not of a single gene.
claims.source: Because the prevalence of SD motifs is a feature of the genome in general and not of a single gene, it makes sense that evolutionary selective pressure for or against SD usage would act at the level of the transcriptome.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that SD usage varies at the genome level.

claims.claim: Bacteria with high levels of SD usage tend to have higher maximal growth rates.
claims.source: The nature of these selective pressures remains unclear, although Hockenberry recently argued that bacteria with high levels of SD usage tend to have higher maximal growth rates (Hockenberry et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Cells were cultured at 37°C in 500 mL of LB + ampicillin (50 mg/L).
claims.source: Unless otherwise specified, cells were cultured at 37°C in 500 mL of LB + ampicillin (50 mg/L).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claims.claim: IPTG was added (0.3 mM final) when the culture reached OD600 = 0.3 and cells were harvested by filtration at OD600 = 0.5.
claims.source: IPTG was added (0.3 mM final) when the culture reached OD600 = 0.3 and cells were harvested by filtration at OD600 = 0.5.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claims.claim: For profiling with retapamulin, cells were harvested 5 min after the addition of retapamulin (100 µg/mL final).
claims.source: For profiling with retapamulin, cells were grown at 37°C in 500 mL of LB + ampicillin to OD600 = 0.3, induced with IPTG, grown to OD600 = 0.45, and then harvested by filtration 5 min after the addition of retapamulin (100 µg/mL final).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

results.result: The authors developed MS2RP (MS2-tagged ribosome profiling), a method to selectively profile mutant ribosomes with altered anti-Shine-Dalgarno (ASD) sequences. Three ASD mutants (S, O, and A) were created, expressed transiently in E. coli, and purified with high purity using MS2 aptamer tagging. The mutant ribosomes can engage in translation but show impaired activity compared to wild-type ribosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C45 collectively establish the MS2RP methodology with appropriate controls. The RT-PCR data (C45, Figure 1C) demonstrates high purity of mutant ribosome isolation. Growth curves (C37), polysome profiles (C38), and rRNA processing analysis (C40) provide evidence that the system is functional. The observation that mutant ribosomes are present but reduced in polysomes (C41-C43) is consistent with their expected impaired function.

results.result: Using MS2RP, the authors reveal for the first time a genome-wide correlation between Shine-Dalgarno (SD) motif strength and ribosome occupancy. While wild-type ribosomes show only weak correlation (C53), ASD mutant ribosomes show robust negative correlation with SD strength (C54). By calculating ΔlogRO (difference between wild-type and mutant), the authors isolate the SD contribution and observe a strong linear positive correlation between SD strength and translation efficiency (C56).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 are well-supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figures 2A-C and supplementary figures. The logic is sound: mutant ribosomes cannot use SD-ASD pairing, so their negative correlation with SD strength reveals that other factors mask SD effects in wild-type profiling. The ΔlogRO analysis effectively isolates the SD contribution. The validation that genes with highest ΔlogRO have strongest SD affinity in the -15 to -6 region (C58) confirms the calculations are capturing genuine SD effects.

results.result: Using retapamulin to trap initiation complexes, the authors demonstrate that mutant ribosomes with altered ASD sequences correctly select annotated start sites genome-wide, even at sites with no predicted affinity for the mutant ASDs and at sites with strong wild-type SD motifs. This indicates that start sites are 'hard-wired' for initiation independent of SD-ASD base pairing, and that SD motifs are not necessary for determining where initiation occurs.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C75 provide compelling evidence through multiple lines of analysis. Individual gene examples (C60-C65, Figures 3A-B) show mutant ribosomes initiate at correct sites. Genome-wide analyses (C66-C67, Figures 3C-D) confirm this pattern. Critical controls include: (1) sites with no affinity for any mutant ASD still show initiation (C69, Figure 3E), (2) sites with strong wild-type SD motifs are still recognized by mutants (C71-C72), and (3) all three different mutant ASDs initiate at the same sites (C70, C73-C74), arguing against serendipitous base-pairing. The convergence of evidence from multiple mutants and multiple site categories strongly supports the conclusion.

results.result: Analysis of non-annotated AUG codons shows that SD-ASD pairing is neither necessary nor sufficient for translational initiation. Non-annotated AUGs with high initiation scores for wild-type ribosomes also show high scores for mutant ribosomes (C78), and the presence of complementary SD-like sequences near AUG codons is not sufficient to recruit mutant ribosomes (C81). Sites that initiate with one ribosome type initiate with all types regardless of ASD sequence (C82-C83).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C86 extend the findings from annotated sites to non-annotated AUGs. The initiation score analysis (Figures 4B-G) shows that: (1) mutant ribosomes are not generally enriched at non-annotated AUGs (C76-C77), (2) the rare non-annotated sites that do show initiation behave the same for all ribosome types (C78, C82-C83), and (3) complementary sequences alone are insufficient (C80-C81). The consistency across multiple mutant ribosomes and the analysis of both high-IS and low-IS sites provide strong support for the conclusion that SD-ASD pairing is neither necessary nor sufficient.

results.result: The authors identify A-rich sequences upstream of start codons as a feature that promotes initiation. Adenosines are enriched 15 nt upstream and 5 nt downstream of annotated start sites compared to non-annotated AUGs (C87). Reporter assays show that replacing A's with U's reduces GFP expression, and replacing A's with C's abolishes expression (C88-C89). A-rich sequences are enriched at annotated start sites across diverse bacterial species, particularly in species lacking SD motifs like Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Flavobacterium johnsoniae (C91-C92).
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 5A, Figure 5—supplement 1) and functional validation through reporter assays (Figure 5D). The probability logos clearly show A enrichment at annotated sites. The reporter assays provide direct functional evidence, though the effect of U substitution is variable (C88). The complete loss of expression with C substitution (C89) is more convincing. The cross-species analysis (C91-C92) strengthens the generality of the finding. However, the mechanism remains unclear (acknowledged in the discussion), and the reporter assays test only four sites.

results.result: mRNA structure surrounding start codons differs between annotated and non-annotated AUGs. Annotated initiation sites have significantly lower mRNA structure for ~30 nt on both sides of the AUG codon, while non-annotated AUGs show consistently high structure across this region. This suggests that local mRNA structure plays a critical role in start codon selection and likely has a causal role in setting initiation rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C97-C98, C101, and C111 are supported by SHAPE-MaPseq data analysis (Figure 5E) and citations to previous studies. The difference in structure between annotated and non-annotated sites is clear in the data. However, there is a causality issue: the authors acknowledge that ribosomes themselves melt structure during translation (C99), so lower structure at annotated sites could be consequence rather than cause. The correlation between in vivo and in vitro structure measurements (C100) partially addresses this, but the causal claim (C101) remains somewhat uncertain.

results.result: A small number of endogenous genes show increased translation with mutant ribosomes when they have complementary SD-like sequences to the mutant ASD. Examples include hemA (10-fold higher with O-ribosomes), rbsK (7-fold), mreB (10-fold), sapA (9-fold with S-ribosomes), and rsmH (4-fold). However, such examples are rare, and the three ASD mutants essentially act as general loss-of-function mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 are supported by specific gene examples shown in Figures 1E and Figure 1—supplement 2. The fold-changes are substantial and the complementarity between mRNA sequences and mutant ASDs is shown. The conclusion that these are rare exceptions (C52) is reasonable given that endogenous genes evolved to interact with the canonical ASD. This result validates the approach and confirms that the mutants can recognize complementary sequences when present, but also establishes that most genes do not have such sequences.

results.result: The authors propose that MS2RP is a versatile method that could be applied to study rRNA variants in bacteria and eukaryotes, characterize rRNA domain functions, and investigate variant rRNA alleles that are expressed differentially in response to environmental changes or developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107 are largely speculative about future applications (C103, C107 explicitly marked as speculation). While the logic is sound that a plasmid-based system could be transferred to other organisms (C102), this has not been demonstrated. The citations to variant rRNA alleles in bacteria and eukaryotes (C104-C106) establish that such variants exist and are interesting, but do not demonstrate that MS2RP will work in these contexts. These are reasonable proposals for future work but are not supported by data in this manuscript.

results.result: The authors propose two possible explanations for why mutant ribosomes show negative correlation with SD strength: (1) wild-type ribosomes may occlude ribosome-binding sites on mRNAs with strong SD motifs, or (2) mRNA structure and other features may outweigh SD motif effects, masking them in conventional profiling studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are explicitly speculative explanations for the observed negative correlation. Both are plausible mechanisms, but the manuscript does not provide data to distinguish between them. The authors acknowledge this uncertainty by presenting both as possibilities. Additional experiments would be needed to determine which mechanism (or combination) is correct.

results.result: The authors discuss potential mechanisms by which A-rich sequences might enhance initiation, including effects on mRNA dynamics/structure, specific interactions with ribosomal components near the start codon (possibly conserved across domains), or interactions with ribosomal protein S1 further upstream. They note that A-rich sequences have been reported to enhance translation in eukaryotic systems and that the Kozak sequence contains a purine at position -3.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C114, C118-C119 are explicitly speculative about mechanisms. The observation that U substitution reduces translation (C113) argues against a simple structural explanation, but the mechanism remains unclear. The citations to eukaryotic A-rich sequences (C117) and the Kozak sequence (C115-C116) provide interesting context but do not establish mechanism. These are reasonable hypotheses for future investigation but lack direct experimental support in this manuscript.

results.result: The introduction and discussion provide extensive background on bacterial translation initiation, SD motifs, regulatory mechanisms, ribosomal protein S1, and the evolutionary variation in SD motif usage across bacterial species. This establishes the context and significance of the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C31, C33, C36, C39, C120-C124 are primarily background knowledge and citations to previous work. These are well-supported by the cited literature and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide appropriate context for understanding the significance of the current findings. The claims about SD motif variation across species (C24-C29) and the evolutionary implications (C122-C124) are particularly important for framing why the current study matters.

results.result: SD motifs are underrepresented within ORFs to avoid spurious initiation at internal start codons.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is supported by citation to Hockenberry et al., 2018. This is established prior work that provides context for understanding the selective pressures on SD motif usage. It supports the interpretation that SD motifs have functional significance even if they are not necessary for start site selection.

results.result: Ribosomes can melt RNA structure during translation, and SHAPE/DMS reactivity measurements in vivo and in vitro are strongly correlated.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by citations to previous studies. These establish important context for interpreting the mRNA structure data, particularly regarding the causality question of whether low structure enables initiation or results from it. The correlation between in vivo and in vitro measurements (C100) suggests structure has some causal role, but does not definitively resolve the issue.

results.result: The methods section describes growth conditions, induction protocols, and retapamulin treatment procedures used in the experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 describe experimental methods that are straightforward and standard. These are adequately documented for reproducibility. The specific conditions (temperature, media, OD600 values, induction times, antibiotic concentrations) are clearly stated.
